    2027 Ducati Desmo450 EDS First look

    Ducati’s street-legal, single-cylinder enduro.

    By Seth Richards
    June 9, 2026
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 0:48
    Instaread

    At last year’s EICMA show, Ducati previewed the Desmo450 EDS, its first street-legal off-roader. Now, it’s here: a hardcore dual sport with desmodromic valve actuation, optional rider aids, and “adaptive maintenance intervals.” It looks mighty impressive. But there’s a catch.

    Based on the Desmo 450MX, the EDS is the third model in Ducati’s off-road lineup. The 450cc engine has been thoroughly reworked for improved tractability, using a lower 12.9:1 compression ratio,compared to 13.5:1 on the MX. It has revised camshafts; a higher-inertia connecting rod assembly with changes made to the crankshaft and flywheel, and smaller 42mm throttle bodies, down from 44mm on the MX. Those changes come at the cost of outright performance with Ducati claiming the EDS produces a claimed 42 hp at 6750 rpm and 33 ft.-lb. of torque at 5750 rpm in stock trim. With the addition of the Ducati Performance Racing Kit, power is boosted to 54 hp. The kit costs only $261.70, so those are 12 cheap ponies, but, alas, the kit is rated for track-only use.

    In order to handle tight singletrack, the gearbox features revised ratios with a shorter first gear, a taller sixth gear, and altered spacing between all other gears. An up-only quickshifter is standard. To cope with the potential for slower riding, the EDS has a radiator fan on its rhomboid-shaped radiators.

    The Desmo450 EDS uses the same frame as the MX, with forged, cast, and extruded sections, but with revised engine mounting points for optimized stiffness. Ducati says the frame weighs just under 20 pounds. The EDS uses a fully adjustable 49mm Showa fork with 12.2 inches of travel and a model-specific spring rate, and a fully adjustable, progressive-link Showa monoshock with 11.9 inches of travel. The braking setup features a Brembo two-piston caliper mounted on a 260mm Galfer disc in the front, and a single-piston caliper and 240mm disc in the rear. The brake pads are unique to the EDS. Ducati claims the EDS weighs 264 pounds when its 2.2-gallon tank is bone dry—that’s 35 pounds heavier than the MX, but street-legal running gear is always going to come with a weight penalty.

    ADVERTISEMENT

    To cope with the bumps and bruises of enduro riding, Ducati swapped out the MX’s magnesium clutch cover, ignition cover, and valve cover for aluminum units. It also comes standard with handguards, engine guards, and LED lighting.

    The EDS takes advantage of the electronic rider aid suite developed for the Desmo450 MX—but, again, the Ducati Performance Racing Kit has to be installed. When it is, the EDS has engine maps, four levels of traction control intervention, launch control, and engine braking control—all of which can be controlled on the handlebars and customized via Ducati’s X-Link app.

    The X-Link app also comes in handy when it’s time to consider maintenance. According to the press release, “a specific algorithm for the Desmo450 calculates a real-time engine stress index based on operating parameters and conditions of use.” The maintenance schedule is adjusted accordingly, and can be viewed on the app, where it also indicates which of two service types the engine requires. The “Mid” service is a top-end rebuild that includes pistons and valve clearance checks. The “Full” service is “a complete engine overhaul.” The press release says the Mid service will likely fall between 90 and 120 hours of engine time, while the Full service will fall between 180 and 240 hours. KTM invented or at the very least widely popularized the enduro-with-lights segment and its 500 EXC-F is the obvious inspiration for the Desmo450 EDS. The KTM’s recommended intervals require a “valve check” at 35 hours and full engine check including a crank inspection at 70 hours, so not a direct comparison but it’s clear buyers in this category are willing to pay to play.

    For average road riders, those intervals may sound ludicrously short. When service intervals are measured in hours, it’s a good indication what kind of machine you’re looking at. Keep in mind, there are essentially two types of dual sport motorcycles. There’s the kind that uses an engine built with streetbike durability and maintenance in its design brief, like the Suzuki DR-Z4S or KTM 390 Enduro R, the latter of which shares its single-cylinder engine with the 390 Duke, 390 SMC R, 390 Adventure, and RC 390. Then there’s the kind that uses a “real” very high performance (ie maintenance-heavy) dirt bike engine that’s essentially a race motor. The EDS is the latter. For the hard core, engine rebuilds are part of the game, and Ducati’s adaptive maintenance interval system offers real value by taking some of the guess work out of the process.

    The Ducati Performance Riding Kit remains the elephant in the room—but a baby elephant, perhaps. If buyers are going to spend $12,995 to purchase the EDS in the first place, spending an extra $260 for the kit looks like a no-brainer: it unlocks 12 extra hp and gives electronic control that comes standard on the competition models. Why not simply give the stock model the added performance and tech? In part, it comes down to homologation.

    According to Richard Kenton, Ducati North America’s technical director, “The Racing Kit enables the EDS to utilize the state-of-the-art electronics that are not permitted on the street-legal-configured EDS 450 due to local emissions standards. The closed-loop DTC [Ducati Traction Control] system has been designed for racing and therefore is not homologated since, under certain circumstances, the ignition curve is modified for torque reduction.”

    Offering the kit as an accessory allows Ducati to offer a single model instead of two separate versions. Accordingly, the single model can serve two distinct customers: one who’s purely riding for leisure, and one who wants to ride competitively. The kit’s low price shows how serious Ducati is about appealing to customers in a category in which it’s not already an established player.

    The Desmo450 EDS will land in select US dealerships August, 2026.

    2027 Ducati Desmo450 EDS Specs

    MSRP: $12,995
    Engine: Liquid-cooled, single-cylinder; 4 valves/cyl., desmodromic actuation
    Displacement: 450cc
    Bore x Stroke: 96.0 x 62.1mm
    Compression Ratio: 12.9:1
    Transmission/Final Drive: 6-Speed / chain
    Claimed Horsepower: 42 hp @ 6,750 rpm
    Claimed Torque: 33 ft.-lb. @ 5,750 rpm
    Fuel System: Electronic fuel injection w/ 42mm throttle bodies
    Clutch: Wet, multiplate w/ up-only quickshifter; hydraulic actuation
    Frame: Aluminum
    Front Suspension: 49mm inverted Showa fork, fully-adjustable; 12.2 in. travel
    Rear Suspension: Showa monoshock, fully-adjustable; 11.9 in. travel
    Front Brake: 2-Piston Brembo caliper, Galfer 260mm disc
    Rear Brake: 1-Piston Brembo caliper, Galfer 240mm disc
    Wheels, Front/Rear: Spoked w/ Takasago Excel rim; 21 x 1.6 in. / 18 x 2.15 in.
    Tires, Front/Rear: Metzeler Karoo 4; 90/90-21 / 140/80-18
    Rake/Trail: 27.3°/4.6 in.
    Wheelbase: 58.8 in.
    Seat Height: 38.2 in.
    Fuel Capacity: 2.2 gal.
    Claimed Weight (No Fuel): 264 lb.
    Contact: ducati.com
